title: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Computational Irreducibility” (from p. 737), p. 739. Scope: any system whose evolution is computationally irreducible

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The assertion can be made exact for individual models, but its unrestricted scope and informal cost comparison prevent a single decisive test. Existing programs permit counterexample searches and special-case proofs, while general computational lower bounds are difficult and cannot be inferred from simulation alone.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define irreducibility for a specified system family as a lower bound on algorithms predicting state at time t relative to direct evolution, then prove the bound or search for faster predictors. A predictor with asymptotically fewer steps refutes the claim for that family; a valid lower-bound proof confirms it there.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite simulation cannot establish an asymptotic lower bound.

No single formal definition of "almost as many" applies across all systems.

General prediction questions can be undecidable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.35
data existence: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram introduces computational irreducibility as the situation in which prediction takes about as much work as the evolution itself. Scored as stated, the sentence is that definition, so a simulation of any particular rule only illustrates it. Public computation supplies examples and does not supply an independent confirming or refuting outcome.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Call a system irreducible only when no predictor uses substantially fewer steps than the system, then ask whether prediction still takes nearly that many steps. That test repeats the definition.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The sentence applies the definition of computational irreducibility to systems already labeled irreducible.

Without a separate criterion for irreducibility, every outcome fits the claim.
